motion: Is religious disagreement evidence against God’s existence?
sourceRestrictions:
# Frozen source and scope

Exact question: Is religious disagreement evidence against God’s existence? Pro is Justin Schieber; con is Randal Rauser. Justin Brierley is the host. The programme’s January 14, 2017 listing establishes identity and date only. Outside scholarship and assessments are unavailable as judging evidence.

The controller read all 1,596 canonical caption events. Canonical event indices are ZERO-BASED, distinct from the maintained reader’s ONE-BASED line labels. The automatic transcript is unchanged. Complete coverage includes excluded introductory and promotional material for boundary auditing only.

Assess events 319–613, 679–1295 and 1338–1567, restricted to primary-speaker argument words. The audible scope is approximately 12:41–1:00:59; caption overlap and mixed events extend the technical window slightly around these handoffs. Event 319 starts with the host’s “of make your case there”, followed by Schieber’s “yes so in”. Event 679 begins with the host’s “to that kind of stuff”, then Rauser says “yeah I like how”. Event 1295 begins with Rauser’s final “evidence”, followed by host break language. Event 1338 begins with host “towards the end of today’s show”, then Schieber’s “sure so”. Event 1567 ends Rauser’s “disagreement that we presently find”, then the host’s “it’s”. None of these host fragments may be scored or quoted as a guest’s words.

Use the explicit editor-approved moderator-context lane. Brierley’s questions, premises, examples, endorsements and summaries are unscored. A guest’s actual answer remains eligible. Do not silently attribute a host argument to a guest or manufacture an opponent reply target for a host prompt. A later guest explicitly adopting a premise may be judged on that guest’s own stated reasoning. Consider unequal prompting and the absence of a further reply opportunity; no penalty merely because a guest did not answer the other’s final reply.

Brierley introduces prevalence of God-belief as possible theistic evidence at 32:49–33:35, presses independent doctrinal convergence using a fine-tuning/design analogy at 49:44–50:10, frames the argument against other evidence at 55:33–56:33, invokes Jesus’s prayer for unity at 58:19–58:52, and offers a UK ecumenical improvement example at 1:00:03–1:00:31. Those are context only. His earlier team-building, salvation and later ad-hoc summaries track arguments already offered by guests; they do not add scored moves. The contract requires a move-by-move moderatorContextAudit.

Schieber’s landlord analogy distinguishes fundamental conflicting religious commitments from trivial disagreements whose resolution can develop virtues. He expressly denies that his argument assumes God personally delivers contradictory revelations: people claim revelation, and the issue is why a God concerned with truth and relationship would not correct consequential errors. Preserve this clarification at 21:59–22:34 and 33:35–34:19 when evaluating Rauser’s response.

At 19:38–22:34 the speaker is Schieber, despite the preceding host question addressing Rauser. First-person reference to the argument, the toddlers example and subsequent host handoff back to Randal establish this attribution. The host at 22:35 attributes the example to Justin. Distinguish Justin Schieber from Justin Brierley everywhere; shared first names alone do not establish ownership. If remaining selected attribution is materially uncertain, mark it below high and require audio verification before adjudication.

Rauser replies with possible sufficient reasons, a team-building exercise, developmental teaching, general moral knowledge and inclusivist judgment according to available evidence. He does not claim all conflicting doctrines are true or that doctrinal knowledge never matters. His grammar example is an analogy for staged learning; caption corruption of the spelling mnemonic is not an argumentative defect.

Schieber frames the case as comparative evidence or best explanation, expressly not logical contradiction, at 29:40–30:16 and 41:53–42:35. Near 56:33–57:32 he explicitly permits other theistic arguments to outweigh it and denies that it makes belief in God irrational by deduction. Do not assign him proof that every possible divine reason is impossible. Rauser need not independently prove God exists; distinguish logical compatibility from comparative explanatory force when evaluating his replies.

Rauser’s exclusivism objection says theism need not require correct doctrines for salvation. Schieber rejects exclusivism as a premise and stresses false beliefs, impaired relationships and tensions among believers, including conflict and parental restrictions. Do not erase the dispute by silently adopting either reconstruction or treat his caliphate example as a claim about all Muslims.

On relationship, Rauser distinguishes propositional knowledge from acquaintance and developmental relationship, using infant–mother and coworker contrasts. Schieber grants some substantive relationship without mutual awareness but ranks freely chosen mutual awareness higher and asks why God would settle for less. Preserve both concessions; do not attribute denial of all infant–parent value or a settled hierarchy that neither defended.

For hypothetical independent doctrinal convergence, Schieber distinguishes broad supernatural belief from detailed doctrines such as Trinity, divine simplicity and atonement. Rauser proposes possible natural convergence and later invokes projection theories and broad cross-cultural similarities. His final separate point is that greater agreement supporting God would not by itself show current disagreement supports atheism. Account for this closing inference independently; do not collapse specificity, generality, logical negation and comparative evidence.

Rauser’s cognitive-wiring/autism claim at 48:33–49:03 and his evolutionary examples are speaker claims, not independently verified facts or a basis for stereotyping. Likewise Schieber’s evolutionary-literature claim and Rauser’s references to Feuerbach, Freud and Marx receive no outside substantiation. Judge only the warrant actually supplied. Named authorities are not automatic evidence of correctness.

Both concluding replies matter: Schieber defends detailed doctrinal specificity against natural convergence at 52:30–53:58 and qualifies cumulative force at 56:33–57:32; Rauser distinguishes higher agreement from current evidence at 55:09–55:28, then discusses continuing Christian differences and charitable dialogue at 58:52–1:00:59. Repetition may be covered without adding a new move, but a new load-bearing distinction must not be lost.

Automatic captions commonly misrecognize names and terms: Rauser, Schieber, theism, abductive, acquaintance, inclusivism, Feuerbach and irenic. Never penalize recognition errors or silently repair exact quotations. Caption events overlap in time; source spans are contiguous text windows whose mixed-speaker fragments need explicit ownership restrictions. No audio check or direct listening has yet occurred. Any selected uncertainty material to attribution or meaning requires below-high confidence and subsequent verification.

Featured quotations must be exact 3–18 word complete thoughts with clear referents and essential qualifications. Do not crop a concession away from its challenge, quote a dangling clause, silently fix caption wording or invent completion words. Select a different complete excerpt if the original will not fit. At least one suitable candidate per side must be available before inventory lock.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: Fundamental incompatible beliefs among devout believers create tension among believers and between believers and God.
moves.warrant: In the landlord analogy, conflicting private-message claims about identity and obligations frustrate clarity and relationships; religious believers likewise report incompatible revelation claims about central matters.
moves.inference: A relational God’s apparent failure to prevent or correct fundamental confusion is evidence calling for explanation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Begins after the mixed host fragment with Schieber’s analogy and ends after he distinguishes fundamental religious questions from trivial disputes.
moves.attributionRationale: The host hands the floor to Schieber, who introduces his own book analogy and continues in first person throughout the selected argument.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is needed for ownership; the named handoff and sustained first-person continuity are clear in the captions.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies the core phenomenon and divine expectation from which the pro motion case begins.

burdenContact.rationale: It specifies how fundamental disagreement allegedly damages the relationship a relational God would seek.

moves.description: Fundamental incompatible beliefs among devout believers resemble tenants receiving conflicting private messages, creating relational tension that a truth-valuing God would seemingly address.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The landlord analogy concretely narrows the target to fundamental conflicts among willing believers and links confusion with impaired divine and interpersonal relationships. Principal limitation: It leaves partly implicit why divine communication inherits a landlord’s clarification duty, while illustrative incompatibilities establish neither prevalence nor representative distribution. Live burden: Schieber must show consequential disagreement is appreciably less expected under relational theism than atheism after admitting plausible goods from limited uncertainty.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: The landlord analogy need not carry over, and Schieber must show why the actual degree of disagreement is beyond what God could permissibly allow.
moves.warrant: A theist may hold that God revealed information to one group and not another rather than issued contradictions, and Schieber already allows that some differential revelation can have sufficient reasons.
moves.inference: Observed disagreement is not by itself a sustainable objection unless its amount and distribution are shown to be evidentially unacceptable.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Covers Rauser’s complete initial response: his challenge to the analogy’s revelation assumption and his linked burden concerning degree and distribution.
moves.attributionRationale: The host explicitly asks Randal for his response, and the answer uses third-person references to Justin while advancing Rauser’s position.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is needed because the named handoff and argumentative continuity make ownership clear.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the con side’s primary challenge to the inference from disagreement to evidence against God.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the raw fact and degree of disagreement do not yet discriminate between theism and atheism.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the analogy’s assumption about divine communication and demands an account of why the actual degree is excessive.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The issue is not that God gives incompatible revelations but that fundamental claimed revelations conflict and a relational God has reasons to correct the resulting misunderstandings.
moves.warrant: The disputes concern salvation, divine nature, history and moral-political requirements, rather than low-stakes matters where self-resolution plausibly builds character.
moves.inference: The seriousness of the errors makes nonintervention harder to explain under theism even without attributing contradictions directly to God.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Includes Schieber’s toddler contrast, catalogue of fundamental disputes, express denial of contradictory divine revelation, and reason for corrective clarification.
moves.attributionRationale: Although the preceding question addresses Rauser, first-person reference to Schieber’s argument, the toddler example, and the later handoff back to Randal establish Schieber as speaker.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The source notes expressly resolve this potentially confusing handoff through first-person continuity; no further audio check is required.
moves.importanceRationale: It preserves a crucial qualification and answers the central misreading of the pro argument.

burdenContact.rationale: It connects consequential error to reasons a truth-valuing relational God would have to clarify matters.

responseComponents.description: Rejects the premise that the argument attributes contradictory revelations to God and specifies why the relevant degree matters.

moves.description: Schieber denies that God issues contradictions, contrasts trivial disputes with salvation, history, divine nature, and political morality, and argues that serious misunderstandings invite correction.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Schieber repairs the central misreading by separating human revelation claims from divine authorship and ties correction to specific high-stakes disputes rather than every doctrinal variation. Principal limitation: The examples establish seriousness more readily than frequency, causal harm, or the probability that a relational God would intervene consistently across cultures, and the record does not quantify how often those errors produce the alleged harms. Live burden: He must explain why development, freedom, accommodation, or other relational goods do not justify these errors at roughly their observed scale.

moves.speaker: Justin Schieber
moves.claim: The team-building analogy supports Schieber because radically different understandings of the task prevent successful cooperation.
moves.warrant: A team cannot combine strengths when each member has different problems, rules and deadlines; an instructor would be expected to clarify the shared goal from the top down.
moves.inference: Fundamental religious disagreement defeats the proposed team-building good unless God provides the clarity that appears absent.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Captures Schieber’s complete reconstruction of the team-building analogy and the resulting demand for top-down clarification.
moves.attributionRationale: The host asks Justin directly, and Schieber explicitly names and reconstructs Randal’s team-building analogy.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is needed because the direct handoff and named target make ownership clear.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the principal pro answer to the con side’s character-building rationale.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that the kind of disagreement observed blocks rather than advances the relational cooperation offered as justification.

responseComponents.description: Refashions the team exercise to show that disagreement over the task itself prevents its proposed benefits.

moves.description: Schieber reverses the team-building analogy: cooperation fails when participants receive incompatible goals, rules, and deadlines, so fundamental religious confusion calls for top-down clarification.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The reconstructed exercise shows disagreement about the shared task disabling cooperation instead of cultivating it, and its rules-goals-deadlines contrast makes that reversal unusually transparent. Principal limitation: It assumes religions lack enough common purpose for collaboration and does not establish that divine guidance must resemble an instructor’s explicit briefing, especially where traditions share broad moral aims despite doctrinal differences. Live burden: Schieber must connect the model to actual fundamental disputes while allowing that partial shared moral aims and guidance may survive.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Disagreement may serve virtue formation and staged divine teaching.
moves.warrant: A team-building task develops character through interpretive tension, while a teacher appropriately gives simplified or differing instruction according to students’ developmental level.
moves.inference: Some religious disagreement can be explained by God’s pedagogical accommodation rather than divine absence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Starts with Rauser’s answer to the host’s request for reasons and includes both his team-building and grammar-teaching analogies through their conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: The host explicitly returns the question to Randal, whose answer supplies examples identified elsewhere in the discussion as his.
moves.audioVerificationReason: No audio verification is needed; the named handoff and later references consistently identify these analogies as Rauser’s.
moves.importanceRationale: This supplies concrete sufficient reasons central to the con route rather than merely asserting possibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It offers observable proposed goods—character formation and developmentally fitted instruction—that could justify permitted disagreement.

responseComponents.description: Offers developmental and character-building reasons why immediate uniform correction may not be required.

moves.description: Rauser proposes that interpretive tension can build character and that a master teacher may provide developmentally fitted instruction, making some disagreement compatible with divine pedagogy.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Rauser supplies two intelligible mechanisms—cooperative formation and staged teaching—rather than resting on a bare assertion that God might possess unknown reasons. Principal limitation: The grammar lesson concerns progressively expanded instruction, whereas disputed doctrines can contradict one another about shared goals, and no evidence connects their distribution to developmental readiness. Live burden: He must show these pedagogical benefits arise from consequential disagreements and plausibly outweigh persistent false belief’s relational costs.

moves.speaker: Randal Rauser
moves.claim: Freedom, general moral knowledge and judgment proportionate to available revelation can mitigate the stakes of religious disagreement.
moves.warrant: Rauser cites value in freely seeking God, a moral law written on human hearts, and the principle that people are judged according to the revelation accessible to them.
moves.inference: Lack of uniform detailed doctrine need not entail unfair divine treatment or the loss of all relevant guidance.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: Excludes the initial mixed host words, then captures Rauser’s three stated reasons and his conclusion about judgment based on accessible revelation.
moves.attributionRationale: After the mixed event’s host fragment, Rauser says he likes the setup and enumerates his own three points.
moves.audioVerificationReason: The mixed boundary is explicitly documented and the scored words begin only with Rauser’s response, so no audio verification is needed.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly addresses alleged relational and salvific harm with an alternative account of responsibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It gives criteria for fair judgment and meaningful guidance despite unequal doctrinal access.

responseComponents.description: Argues that consequences of error are mitigated when judgment tracks accessible knowledge and general moral awareness.

moves.description: Rauser combines freedom to seek God, general moral knowledge, and judgment proportionate to available revelation to mitigate unfairness despite unequal doctrinal access.

moves.description: Rauser concedes serious Christian divisions, suggests providential ambiguity can promote charitable inquiry, and cites ecumenical listening as relational value realized through continued disagreement.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Rauser treats the objection seriously, names concrete disputes, and grounds a proposed benefit in ecumenical experience, producing a charitable and limited final response. Principal limitation: Dialogue goods and possible providential reasons do not justify the observed amount or consequences of ambiguity, nor answer every truth-based corrective challenge, particularly where ambiguity concerns initiation, sacrament, or salvation rather than harmless diversity. Live burden: Rauser must show these benefits make fundamental division expected under God rather than merely compatible with permission.
